newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover protest to focus on Tiananmen killing.
newsitem.headline: HK handover protest to focus on Tiananmen killing.

text.p: Pro-democracy demonstrators said on Tuesday they plan to highlight the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre during protests coinciding with the transfer of this wealthy British colony to Communist China later this month.

The Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democracy Movements in China, Hong Kong's largest pro-democracy grouping, said it would show a video of the bloody repression outside the convention hall where the handover ceremonies will take place on June 30.
"We will demand the release of pro-democracy prisoners, the punishment of those responsible for June 4 events and the end of single-party rule (in China)," Alliance leader Szeto Wah said.
Beijing sent tanks to crush a mass student demonstration for greater democracy in Tiananmen Square in June 1989, leading to heavy loss of life and stunning many Hong Kong residents.

Pro-democracy protesters have vowed to exploit the elaborate handover festivities, grouping some 4,000 guests and 8,000 journalists, to focus world attention on efforts to limit their freedoms and China's human rights record.
Prince Charles, heir to the British throne, will hand back the colony of 6.4 million residents to China's President Jiang Zemin at midnight on June 30, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Szeto, speaking near the colonial legislature, said Alliance demonstrators would not chant "Down with Li Peng" during their handover protests. He was referring to China's prime minister.
Hong Kong Justice Minister-designate Elsie Leung said this week anyone chanting "Down with Li Peng" would be committing sedition if they were inciting the overthrow of the government.
Leung will be sworn in on July 1 after China takes control and will then decide whether demonstrators have broken restrictions on protests imposed by a new pro-Beijing assembly.
Police on Tuesday said they were setting up two areas for demonstrations near the central convention centre where the handover ceremonies will take place.
The locations could accommodate about 300 people, a far cry from the 55,000 people who turned out at the Alliance's request this year on the anniversary of Tiananmen.
"I hope organisers, demonstrators or individuals come forward as early as possible because we have very limited spaces around the place," police chief Dick Lee told reporters.
Lee said no police permit would be needed for the two-day period from June 30 to July 2 but protesters must notify police of their plans.
In effect, police appeared to be giving protesters a two-day handover grace period, since curbs on demonstrations will be voted into law early on July 1 by the new pro-Beijing assembly.
Lee said police expected to receive new instructions after the new assembly votes but these regulations would not apply to protests from June 30 to July 2 if a notification was made now.

The main point of contention remains plans by the Democratic Party to occupy the gallery of the colonial legislature building and read out a protest statement while the pro-Beijing assembly is being sworn in on handover night.

The office of Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-Hwa has agreed to be flexible about the plan. However, he called on the Democrats on Tuesday not to occupy the building and its balcony but to protest outside. His call was echoed by members of the new legislature.
